chapter: Los Angeles, Central Avenue and the Apex
title: White-owned businesses fronted by blacks on Central Avenue
summary: Central Avenue was the heart of black entertainment, yet most businesses were owned by whites and fronted by blacks.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: So far as music and entertainment went, though, the heart of black entertainment (Unintelligible) --
Would always be 40th and Central Avenue, even though Central Avenue wasn't all black, is that right?
Well, outward, it would give the appearance of being like 75 or 80 percent black, but I would say 75

percent of the businesses or 80 percent of the businesses that were owned in the Central Avenue area were owned by Caucasians. I'm all mixed up with my words. But the Caucasians were the ones that owned it and a lot of times they had black guys fronting the businesses for them, because it takes money to run businesses and if you don't have it, you must get. So they got.
So, most of the places, businesses, were actually owned by whites and fronted by blacks.
